The narrow-gauge line from Pell to Tarsel climbs nine hundred metres in fourteen kilometres, on rails and curves its builders laid out for slow, heavy wagons. It was built in 1911 to carry the cheese of Tarsel's farms down to the market at Pell, a trade it still exists to serve. Two years ago the council changed the timetable. The first train now leaves Pell at ten, an hour that suits the visitors from the Pell hotels, and the farmers, whose cheese must reach the market by nine, have taken to sending it down the valley road by truck.

At Gessen, halfway up, the train pauses for ten minutes so that the visitors can photograph the viaduct across the Lenn gorge, which is best seen from the halt. The Hollin, the line's steam engine, took on water at Pell and needs none here. Ilse Marran, with her engine ready and the minutes to fill, stands on the platform and whistles a scale, up and down, until the cameras are put away. Above her, goats graze the scree slope, where a stone wall that the council rebuilt in 2015, and paid for itself, holds back the loose rock.

The farmers are the ones who lose by the change. At Tarsel I watched a farmer load his cheese onto a truck twenty metres from the station, because the train would have reached Pell three hours after the market opened, and the Gessen farms send their cheese down the road as well. In winter, when the visitors stay away, the trains stand in the shed at Pell, and the snowploughs keep the road open for everything else.

None of this needed to happen. A line built to serve the village's farmers now runs at the hours that suit the hotels, and the farmers are left to hire trucks. The council should put the first train back at dawn, load the cheese, and give the visitors the second train, which would still reach Gessen in good light for their photographs.

Ostley's open-air pool opened in 1936 beside the Ost, with a diving tower at the deep end and a pike picked out in blue tiles on the basin floor. It closed in 2019, after a winter flood cracked the basin. The swimming club petitioned the council to put the tiles back under the water. Of the four designs entered, Teodora Lind's would cost more than two of its rivals and take a summer longer than the quickest, but it was the only one with a café on the terrace.

That café is a glass box on the west corner of the terrace, the sunniest spot in the pool, and Lind set the old tiles into its back wall. The floor of the new basin is plain white. The cracked old basin was crushed into the concrete of the terrace. The pumps sit beneath the terrace's east end. The swimming club, which had offered to buy the tiles one by one, was told they were wanted for the café. The diving tower has been repainted at the council's expense, and a flood wall now stands between the basin and the river.

On opening day the town band struck up, and at the first bar of the old swimming march the club dived in together. By three o'clock the terrace was half empty, because the café's glass walls throw a long shadow across it. The café should have gone by the north gate, where its shadow would have fallen on the car park.

In the café hangs a photograph of opening day in 1936: boys crowding the tower, the swimming club posed on its steps, the terrace full in the afternoon sun, the Ost running a few yards from the edge, and the pike dark beneath the surface. Look at the terrace in that picture: every seat faces west, into the late sun, because that was when the town came to swim after work.

Putting a glass box on the sunny end of a west-facing terrace was the wrong decision, made for the sake of the café's takings. The pike belongs under the water, and the café belongs at the gate.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. Now they are saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine, colours Councillor Mara Varga picked herself from a paint card in her office. A class at Larch Street School had sent the council a careful scheme matching each bridge to a bus line, so that commuters could tell the bridges apart and find the right one, and it went into a drawer.

What the bridges needed this summer was repair, not paint. Every spring the city's inspectors ring cracks in coloured chalk, yellow for watch and red for mend, and this April the railings of the plum and teal bridges carried eleven red rings. Those repairs, already logged by the inspectors, were put off to next year, and the parks crew's orders were to paint straight over the chalk. Residents had asked in an online vote for the railings to come first.

The paint came from Holm & Daughters, whose stock rose on the exchange the week the order was announced. The whole bill came to a third of the cost of mending the cracks, and the council signed it off in a single evening. Visitors have since come down to the river to photograph the spans, a side effect Councillor Varga now mentions in every interview.

The crew can hardly be blamed. They worked fast, losing a day to a mix-up at the depot, which misread an order and sent the coral tins to the wrong bridge, and a few more to rain on the bare concrete. In 2019 the city planned to paint every bridge the same green, and that plan was shelved for want of money; this one found its money by taking it from the railings.

The city should have mended the railings in the spring and painted the bridges next year, in whatever colours its residents and its schoolchildren chose. Instead it has put a bright coat over eleven red rings and called the job finished.

Every June Kesterby closes Moss Lane to cars and sends its riders two kilometres uphill from the stone bridge, past the old chapel and the war memorial, to the green. Halfway up waits a bend named the Knuckle, a hundred metres of cobbled stones so steep that strong riders stand on their pedals. Beside it, behind a gate, runs Pell's smooth farm track, curving round the bend.

By custom Hettie Varn, the organiser, sounds the handbell for every rider who reaches the green, the last rider as long as the winner. The field included Arlo Maske, eleven times champion, whose first winning time, 9:41 in 1988, is still the record, though he expects some youngster to break it any June now. He leaves talk of a twelfth win to others. He had lifted sixteen-year-old Jory Penhale's old steel bicycle and called it heavy but fit for any hill. Before the start Arlo chalked Nell Odrey's name at the top of the pub blackboard of tips.

This year the committee changed the one rule: to make the climb less daunting for newcomers, riders could take Pell's farm track around the Knuckle. Most did, Jory among them. He passed Arlo outside the old chapel, swung onto the track while Arlo hauled himself up the cobbles, and came past the war memorial alone to reach the green in 9:52, a winning time well outside the champion's record. Nell Odrey finished third. A hill climb that lets riders go around its hardest bend fails to test the one thing it exists to test.

The finish line had been painted inside the show ring on the green, where ponies were judged that morning, and Hettie stood at its rail with the handbell. Moss Lane was laid with tarmac in 1964, all but the Knuckle, whose loose stones volunteers reset each spring, keeping it as firm as when the first race was run in 1961.

The committee should have kept the Knuckle compulsory for every rider and given newcomers a shorter course of their own. Instead it has made Kesterby's one real test optional, and a test that riders may skip measures nothing.

March 2. Ms. Fenn says contest letters must be typed on a manual typewriter, with a deadline of Friday the thirteenth. Gran bought an old machine at a rummage sale last spring and set it on a shelf, booklet in the lid, repair tag on the handle. The carriage had stopped working, and Dad, certain it could be mended, found its spring snapped in two. He brought oil from the garage. My cousin Juno, who first saw a typewriter at school this term, shrugged.

March 4. I carried the machine to Mr. Ostrow, the old repairman on Keel Street, whose shop Juno has walked past all her life without going in. Mr. Ostrow remembered the typewriter the moment he saw the tag: he had cleaned it every autumn for a schoolteacher on Mill Lane, thirty years ago. He took a spring from a broken machine and showed me where it would hook. When I tried to pay, he waved the coins away; he wanted only to see it working again.

March 5. Back at the shop after school, Mr. Ostrow stood beside me through every step of fitting the spring; on my own I would have bent the hook. Gran lent me her pastry brush for the dust, and her spare ribbon still had ink in it. Even Juno said I was too close now to give up. Mr. Ostrow is closing the shop, he told me, because he lacks the capital to renew the lease.

March 7. The sign in the Keel Street window came down yesterday, and the shelves are bare. I typed my opening sentence and then sat for a long time turning the old repair tag from his shop over in my fingers. Its ink has faded to the colour of weak tea.

March 9. I posted the letter this morning, four days before the deadline, typing every line with the even stroke Mr. Ostrow taught me. Juno spends her lunch hours at the school's one typewriter now, and on Friday she asked Ms. Fenn how many words the contest allows. She says she would rather use that machine than borrow mine.
